intended_object: The Weyl module 𝕊^μ(kⁿ) (Fulton–Harris, Lecture 6): the image of the Young symmetrizer c_t of a μ-tableau t acting on (kⁿ)^{⊗|μ|} by permuting tensor factors, viewed as a GL_n(k)-subrepresentation of the tensor power. Inferred from the docstring and the module documentation.
explanation:
The body is `tensorPowerRange (stdRep k n) μ.card (youngSymmetrizerOver k t)`. Here `tensorPowerRange` is the range of a group-algebra element acting on the tensor power through `PiTensorProduct.reindexRepresentation`, packaged as a subrepresentation. `stdRep` is GL_n(k) acting on kⁿ by matrix–vector multiplication. `youngSymmetrizerOver` is c_t = a_t·b_t (row symmetrizer times column antisymmetrizer) over ℚ, pushed into k along `algebraMap ℚ k`. So the definition is exactly Im(c_t) ⊆ (kⁿ)^{⊗d}, which is Weyl's construction.

Whether permutations act on the left or the right only swaps c_t for a conjugate-type element, and the resulting modules are isomorphic. The library's own lemmas back this up: the module is independent of the tableau up to isomorphism, it vanishes exactly when μ has more than n rows, and the extreme shapes give Sym^d and ⋀^d. The ℚ-algebra hypothesis is the characteristic-zero setting in which this construction gives the classical Weyl/Schur module, and the module docstring explains why it is there. In positive characteristic the image of a symmetrizer is not the standard modular Weyl module, so a ℚ-algebra is a reasonable setting here, not an artificial restriction.

Restricting to V = kⁿ with GL_n(k) is the standard setting for Weyl modules as GL_n-representations, and the docstring says plainly that only the value at kⁿ is built, not the functor. The general "image of a group-algebra element on a tensor power of any representation" is already available as `tensorPowerRange`. Mathlib has no Schur functor or Weyl module to cite as a broader counterpart.
